reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: Characteristic features are swollen, spongy, bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, and easy bruising
Impaired collagen formation causes poor wound healing, reopening of old scars, and painful subperiosteal or joint haemorrhages
It should be suspected in people with very restricted diets, chronic alcohol use, severe mental illness, isolation, or malabsorption
In infants and children it can cause painful pseudoparalysis from subperiosteal bleeding and bone changes
A normocytic or, with associated deficiencies, mixed anaemia is common
Symptoms respond rapidly and dramatically to restoration of dietary vitamin C, which strongly supports the diagnosis
The diagnosis is largely clinical and dietary, since the vitamin is abundant in fresh fruit and vegetables and deficiency reflects their prolonged absence
reference.pathophysiology: Ascorbic acid is a cofactor for enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine residues, a step essential for stable collagen cross-linking. Deficiency yields defective, unstable collagen, weakening blood vessel walls, connective tissue, bone matrix, and wound repair, which manifests as haemorrhage, gum disease, and impaired healing. Vitamin C also acts as an antioxidant and aids intestinal iron absorption, so deficiency can contribute to anaemia. Humans cannot synthesise the vitamin and body stores are limited, so deficiency develops after weeks to months without dietary intake.
additionalDifferentials: Gingivitis or periodontal disease from other causes
Child abuse (mimicked by bone and periosteal changes in children)
additionalInvestigations: Careful dietary history for prolonged lack of fruit and vegetables
Plasma or leucocyte ascorbic acid level where available
Full blood count and iron studies for associated anaemia
Coagulation and platelet studies to exclude a primary bleeding disorder
Radiographs in children showing characteristic metaphyseal and subperiosteal changes
redFlags: Significant haemorrhage, including gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding
Painful pseudoparalysis in a child from subperiosteal haemorrhage
Profound weakness and collapse in advanced deficiency
Coexisting severe malnutrition requiring broader nutritional support
reference.prognosis: Excellent with restoration of vitamin C intake; bleeding and gum changes resolve within days to weeks and full recovery is expected.
pitfalls: Attributing bleeding gums or purpura to a primary haematological disorder and missing the dietary cause
Failing to take an adequate dietary history in at-risk individuals
Misinterpreting childhood bone changes as trauma or abuse
Overlooking coexisting deficiencies in a globally malnourished patient
management: Restore vitamin C with ascorbic acid replacement (oral where tolerated) as the definitive treatment
Correct the underlying dietary deficit with vitamin C-rich fruit and vegetables and dietitian input
Provide analgesia for painful subperiosteal and joint haemorrhages, with gentle handling of children who have pseudoparalysis
Treat coexisting anaemia, including iron supplementation for associated iron deficiency
Offer gingival and dental care for spongy, bleeding gums
Address contributory factors such as chronic alcohol use, eating disorders, social isolation or malabsorption
Monitor clinical response, expecting rapid resolution of bleeding and gum changes
